3. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioners, seriously challenged the impugned order of rejection and submitted that the genuineness of the sale deeds executed by the defendant No. 1 has been questioned in the plaint as well as in some Other applications of the plaintiff opposite party, so it is necessary for the defendant-petitioners to establish their case of purchase of the suit property as pleaded in the written statement, as the onus of proving the pleadings of the respective parties does never shift. The petitioners, as well as the defendant No. 1 who is dead, of course have in their written statements seriously challenged the genuineness of the alleged bainapatra upon which the present suit has been instituted. So far the proof of genuineness of the said bainapatra the onus is however upon the plaintiff-opposite party. But so far the genuineness of the purchase deeds of the defendant-petitioners which have been executed by defendant No. 1 Nihar Bala by putting her LTI, the defendant petitioners should not be shut out from establishing the same by expert's opinion after examination and comparison of the LTI of the executant Nihar Bala by a finger-print expert which the defendant petitioners want to do in the interest of justice. He further submits that it is true that the learned Subordinate Judge is quite competent under section 73 of the Evidence Act to compare the LTI of the executant Nihar Bala appearing in the aforesaid sale-deeds with her other LTIs available in the record of the suit, but in the facts and circumstances of the case, it will be better to have an expert's opinion by examination and comparison of the LTI of the defendant No. 1 appearing in the sale-deeds with those admitted and available in some other papers of the suit and to thus enable the court to come to a correct decision as to the claim of the defendant petitioners for the suit property by purchase by the registered deeds in question, particularly when there is provision under section 45 of the Evidence Act for examination of LTI by experts. In support of his contention he has relied upon some decisions reported in 28 DLR 123 and AIR 1928 (PC) 277. In the case reported in AIR 1928 (PC) 277 it has been observed, inter alia that "mere comparison of admitted signature without expert's advice or microscopic examination, is dangerous". In the decision reported in 28 DLR 123, it has been observed that "expert's opinion enables the court to come to a satisfactory conclusion, though the said opinion is not binding upon the court." It is true that the court itself can compare any signature or LTI of any concerned person himself under section 73 of the Evidence Act and come to a decision but it is better to have an expert's opinion also particularly in case of LTI. 

 4. Mr. ABM Nurul Islam the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party, however, supports the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge and submits that the main document relating to the subject matter of the suit, is the bainapatra. Referring to sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act, he submits that the sole onus is upon the plaintiff to prove whether the said bainapatra is genuine or not, The genuineness of the alleged purchase deeds of the defendant-petitioners is not so much relevant and important in the suit and as such the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly rejected the prayer of the defendant-petitioners for examination of the thumb impression i.e. LTI of the defendant No. 1 by a finger print expert. We have heard the learned Advocates, considered their submissions and perused the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge and we find much substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we feel that the defendant-petitioners should not be deprived of the opportunity of proving their case as pleaded in their written statement, particularly when they have offered to bear all the expenses for examining the LTI of the defendant No. 1 in the documents concerned by a finger print expert and when there is no chance of the plaintiff opposite party being prejudiced in any way.
